newsitem.title: USA: WALL ST WEEK AHEAD/FOMC, triple witching.
newsitem.headline: WALL ST WEEK AHEAD/FOMC, triple witching.

text.p: Wall Street enters the week still smarting from last week's drubbing and analysts predict the faint of heart are likely to be tested again this week.

On Tuesday, the Federal Reserve's Open Market Committee (FOMC) will conduct its monthly interest rate policy meeting and even though just about no one is expecting an increase in rates, the session always raises worries.
"There's always concern when the Fed meets," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany. "But I don't think there are any expectations of a change in policy."

This particular meeting may draw particular scrutiny because the selling wave now afflicting stocks began after a recent speech by Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan, during which he rhetorically raised a question about "irrational exuberance" in the market.
Since that speech the Dow has worked its way steadily lower, falling sharply in three of the six sessions that followed.
A second wrinkle will develop over the course of the week, as Friday's quarterly "triple-witching" expiration of options, index options and futures approaches.

Analysts said trying to predict the market outlook during a triple-witching period -- when institutions square massive positions -- is an exercise in futility, particularly when the market is already showing volatility ahead of the expirations.
"You don't even have a clue until two or three days before as to how things are going to go," said Peter Canelo, chief investment strategist at Dean Witter.
"Sometimes if you see a rally leading in, you can theorize that dealers are short," he said, "but the markets have been so choppy lately that I don't know if you could make any statement about it."
Analysts did predict that as the week progressed, the program trading that has buffeted the Dow lately is likely to intensify, yielding an even more volatile market.

For those able to listen through the background noise of triple-witching and the FOMC, there are some indicators analysts will eye to guage whether the recent sell-off is anything more than a short-lived correction.
"I think the weekly mutual fund data will be closely watched to see if we have any more redemptions," said Richard Cripps, chief market strategist at Legg Mason Wood Walker.
Investors have shown time and time again during the bull market a willingness to buy on every dip, and for that reason, Cripps said, the next several sessions could be key.

"I don't know if I can give any evidence yet, but my sense is it's different this time," he said. "For one thing, the real serious bargain hunting that usually takes place during (year-end) tax-loss selling doesn't seem to be taking place."
The week offers a light calendar of economic reports, with industrial production, capacity utilization and housing start data due early in the week.

"I'm crossing my fingers because those reports could set the tone for the bond market if there's any surprise," Johnson said. "I think some of the hysteria will have subsided when we start the week but the market will still be very, very guarded and a lot more sober."

Any reluctance to feed new money into the market would be taken as a sign confidence is waning, but some still insist that as long as the economic fundamentals are favorable, the bulls should remain in charge.

"I think the market's basically been looking for an excuse to take profits," Canelo said. "But as long as there's no real risk of interest rates changing I don't think there's any fundamental problem."
